chapter: Tenor players, tours and band boys
title: Band boys: Russell, Harold Holden and Rudolph Rillis
summary: They recall Lucky's fashion-plate valet Russell and Cab's valets, with Rudolph Rillis the epitome of the band boy.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x:
If you have anything that you
really particularly wanted to talk about now, I'd like to
read you some puns about some of the cats -- what about some
of these band boys we had -- every band, we always had a band boy.

We had a band boy with us when I was
with Lucky, named Russell. He was a fashion plate. This
cat outdressed everybody in the band, and he was the only
valet I knew that didn't want to get his hands dirty.

Now the band boy is supposed to take
care of all the musical instruments and the uniforms, right?
He got him a valet -- a guy named
Speedy who used to work for Chick Webb. But he got Speedy to take care of the band, and all he did was take care of Lucky.

So he used to be standing on the corner looking like a fashion plate; in fact, people used to think he was one of the musicians because he looked more like a musician than we did. And you know how they used to do when they'd get to those hotels; they'd sit up there and con the people to get a free room --
Yeah, because he wasn't making as much money as the musicians, so he had to really hustle hard.
Yes, he hustled hard. He really did, too.

When he'd go in to the restaurant to buy sandwiches for us, he'd have (Inaudible) get him one. I remember when I first came with Cab Calloway, he had a band boy named Harold Holder, the same type as you were just mentioning -- a very sharp cat, very intelligent man; a good dresser, and very dignified. He was Cab Calloway's personal valet, and another kid who you know, and of course, I know, which we consider, or at least I consider, the epitome of all band boys and valets was Rudolph Rillis.
Rudolph Rillis, that is right -- he was THE band boy.
But Rudolph Rillis was the band boy for the band when I came in to Cab's band, and then when Harold Holden

married managed some lady that was with Ebony Magazine or something, because I would say he was a sharp dude, you know, and he finally got to work with a nice lady, and a very brilliant person -- and when he left, Rudolph inherited the job as band boy to Cab Calloway, and he got Paul Parker.
Yeah, as his assistant.
And Paul was another slick one; he was a big ladies' man. But go ahead and talk about these cats, now, will you?
Oh, I usually sit back, now that I have to set up my own drums, I used to just love to walk in and see my drums all set up, and all I had to do was to just move a few things around.
That's right. But them days are gone now.

That's right. Now I have to do all this myself, I got to pick up those drums, and at the time when this was happening, when they set up my drums, I was young and strong and full of energy. Now, -- now that I have one foot in the grave, I got to do it myself.

The same with me -- I have to set up my bass, take the cover off, and then I got to go out and take a nap before I can come back and play! But we always agreed that Rudolph was the epitome of a band boy, because he would have the uniforms all out for us, he assigned our dressing rooms, remember that?
He knew his job well.
He knew who roomed with who so they'd be compatible; he wouldn't get the wrong guys together.
He knew his job well. I mean any time you speak of band boys, you take Rudolph and put him over on the side and then you start talking about the other guys.
Oh, he was the epitome of a band boy.
Right.
